extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in differential geometry and Ricci flow
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style exposition of Perelman's Li–Yau type estimate, the Li–Yau path integral, the Li–Yau–Perelman reduced distance and reduced volume, their differential inequalities and monotonicity, and applications (Jacobian comparison and no-local-collapsing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shrinking gradient Ricci soliton (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A shrinking gradient Ricci soliton gij with potential f satisfies (2.6.1) Rij + ∇i∇j f − (1/2τ) gij = 0 (with τ = −t and t < 0). Taking trace yields R + Δf − n/(2τ) = 0 (eqn (2.6.2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is introduced as the basic model for which the Li–Yau and Li–Yau–Hamilton quantities vanish; subsequent identities (e.g., (2.6.3), (2.6.4)) and normalizations (setting certain constants to zero) are derived from this definition and used repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backward heat equation / conjugate heat equation equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: The potential f satisfies a backward heat equation (2.6.6); equivalently u = (4πτ)^{-n/2} e^{-f} satisfies the conjugate heat equation ∂u/∂τ − Δu + R u = 0 (eqn (2.6.7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence is used to connect Perelman's Li–Yau type estimate for f with heat-kernel-type estimates for u and to apply maximum-principle arguments to H (the Li–Yau–Hamilton quadratic) via u.

rubrics_metrics.name: Li–Yau–Hamilton quadratic / Perelman H quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: H is the Li–Yau–Hamilton type quadratic: a specific combination of second-order spatial derivatives (or the time derivative), first-order spatial derivatives and zeroth-order terms (see e.g. the identity obtained by combining (2.6.2) and (2.6.3)). For shrinking gradient Ricci solitons the quantity vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives explicit algebraic forms (e.g. (2.6.8)) and shows H appears naturally when expressing the equations for f and u; H is central to deriving monotonicity and comparison inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity of τH (Perelman's Li–Yau estimate)
rubrics_metrics.description: From Lemma 2.6.1 and the evolution equations one gets ∂(τH)/∂τ = Δ(τH) − (2τ)·(positive quadratic terms) − (1/τ)τH (displayed in the lemma), so by the maximum principle max(τH) is nonincreasing in τ and in the fundamental-solution limit one concludes H ≤ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Li–Yau type estimate (H ≤ 0) is the analytic input for the Li–Yau path integral and for deriving reduced distance / heat-kernel estimates; the text remarks proofs of limiting behavior are omitted but references are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: L-length (Li–Yau path integral length)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a space-time curve γ(τ) joining p = γ(0) to q = γ(¯τ), the L-length is defined by L(γ) = ∫_0^{¯τ} √τ (R(γ(τ),τ) + |γ̇(τ)|^2_{g(τ)}) dτ (see beginning of §3.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: L-length is the action whose minimizers define L-geodesics; minimizing L over curves yields the reduced distance. It is the parabolic analogue of energy/length used in the Li–Yau path integral argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced distance / Li–Yau–Perelman distance l(q,τ)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reduced distance is defined by l(q,¯τ) = (1/(2√¯τ)) inf_γ L(γ), where the infimum is taken over all space curves γ(τ), 0 ≤ τ ≤ ¯τ, joining p to q (eqns (2.6.9)–(2.6.10) and §3.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perelman introduced this reduced distance (also called reduced length in related literature); it plays the role of a space-time distance in monotonicity formulas and singularity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: L-geodesic (Euler–Lagrange equation for L)
rubrics_metrics.description: An L-geodesic γ (a critical point of L) satisfies the L-geodesic equation (3.2.1): ∇_X X − (1/2)∇R + (1/(2τ)) X + 2 Ric(X,·) = 0 (where X = γ̇).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence of minimizing L-geodesics between given endpoints is asserted (with standard barrier/distribution arguments when minima are not unique); multiplying by √τ gives a convenient form used for estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: First variation identities for L
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 3.2.1 gives the first variation formula for L; in particular ∇_q L(q,¯τ) = 2√¯τ X(¯τ) and L(q,¯τ) gradient/time-derivative identities (see (3.2.2)), and |∇ L|^2 relates to 4¯τ|X|^2 and curvature terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identities tie the spatial gradient and time derivative of L (and hence of l) to the velocity X of minimizing curves and appear repeatedly in deriving differential inequalities for l and L.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second variation / index form and Hessian estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 3.2.2 computes δ^2_Y L and defines an index form I(V,V) (integral involving curvature, ∇_X V, and derivatives of R). Proposition 3.2.3 gives a Hessian bound: Hess L(Y,Y) ≤ (1/√¯τ) − 2√¯τ Ric(Y,Y) − ∫_0^{¯τ} √τ Q(X,Y) dτ, where Q(X,Y) is a Li–Yau–Hamilton quadratic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The index form controls second variations; equality occurs iff Y is an L-Jacobian field (variation by L-geodesics). These estimates are used to bound ΔL and deduce comparison theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplacian estimate for L (Corollary 3.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summing Hessian estimates gives (in distribution sense) Δ L ≤ n/√¯τ − 2√¯τ R − (1/¯τ) K (equation (3.2.10)/Corollary 3.2.4), where K = ∫_0^{¯τ} (3/2) τ^{1/2} Q(X) dτ. Equality holds everywhere iff the solution is a gradient shrinking soliton satisfying Rij + (1/(2√¯τ)) ∇i∇j L = (1/(2¯τ)) g_ij.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Laplacian bound is a key analytic inequality feeding into subsequent evolution inequalities for l and into monotonicity of reduced volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential inequalities for reduced distance l (Lemma 3.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For l = L/(2√¯τ) one has (in distribution sense) the relations (3.2.11)–(3.2.13): formulas relating ∂l/∂¯τ, |∇ l|^2, and Δ l with curvature R, ¯τ, and the K-term (integral of Q); the inequality Δ l ≤ −l/¯τ + R + (1/(2¯τ^{3/2}))K is among them. Equality characterizes gradient shrinking solitons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These PDE inequalities are the analytic core used to prove bounds on l (e.g., min l ≤ n/2) and to derive monotonicity of the reduced-volume integrand via integration by parts and maximum principle arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum bound for reduced distance (Corollary 3.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a compact n-dimensional manifold evolving by Ricci flow, for any fixed basepoint p and all τ ≥ 0 one has min_{q∈M} l(q,τ) ≤ n/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows by considering  = 4τ l and applying the maximum principle to the combined evolution/inequality derived in Lemma 3.2.5; it is used in volume and noncollapsing arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perelman's reduced volume (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For compact M, Perelman's reduced volume is ˜V(τ) := ∫_M (4πτ)^{-n/2} e^{-l(q,τ)} dV_τ(q), where dV_τ is the volume element of metric g(τ) (definition just before §3.2 end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quantity is the parabolic analogue of heat-kernel-weighted volume (and Huisken's monotonicity for mean curvature flow); it is the central monotone quantity for analyzing Ricci flow singularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian comparison theorem for reduced-volume element (Theorem 3.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Along an L-geodesic γ(τ) starting at a fixed p, the reduced-volume element (4πτ)^{-n/2} e^{-l(τ)} J(τ) (where J is the L-Jacobian) is nonincreasing in τ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is obtained by combining the differential inequalities for l with an estimate for d/dτ log J (inequality (3.2.14)); it is the local statement whose integration proves monotonicity of the total reduced volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity and finiteness of Perelman's reduced volume (Theorem 3.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For complete solutions with bounded curvature (or compact M), ˜V(τ) is finite and nonincreasing in τ; the monotonicity is strict unless the flow is a gradient shrinking soliton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finiteness is shown by approximating near τ = 0 via the exponential map and Gaussian integral; monotonicity follows from Jacobian comparison and integration over TpM. The equality case characterizes solitons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: κ-noncollapsed at scale r (Definition 3.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Ricci-flow solution g(t) is κ-noncollapsed at (x0,t0) on scale r if: whenever |Rm|(x,t) ≤ r^{-2} for all x in B_{t0}(x0,r) and t in [t0−r^2,t0], then Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x0,r)) ≥ κ r^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard noncollapsing condition used in Ricci-flow singularity analysis; it gives a lower bound on volumes under local curvature control and is the property established by Perelman's no-local-collapsing theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: No local collapsing theorem I (Perelman) (Theorem 3.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Ricci flow starting from any metric on a compact n-manifold M, there exist positive constants κ and ρ0 such that the solution is κ-noncollapsed at every point (x0,t0) and for all scales less than ρ0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem is proved using monotonicity of reduced volume and is a cornerstone result: it provides local injectivity-radius/volume lower bounds that persist through the flow and are robust under surgery.
